CSS shapes lit as solid objects

The pieces below are buttons and boxes whose outlines come from corner-shape, border-shape and clip-path: shape(). A fragment shader treats each picture's alpha channel as the height of a solid and lights it: the edges are bevelled, and each piece casts a shadow with its own outline. Move the pointer or drag a finger across the panel to move the light. Press the pieces.

Show the code alpha → height → light
  1. The markup. Each piece that is lit has fx="solid". The keypad is one piece: its seven keys share a canvas.
  2. The outlines, in CSS.
  3. The shader. Sixteen samples of alpha around each pixel give a height and a slope. The slope is the surface normal.
  4. The light, as two custom properties.
  5. Pressing, as a CSS transition.
  6. The page script. It connects the pointer and the tilt sensor to the two properties.
  7. The tilt sensor.
  8. Inside the fx library: the upload and the draw.

How it works

  • The fx library moves each piece into a canvas and gives the shader the piece's picture as a texture with premultiplied alpha. Whatever CSS does to the outline is already in the alpha channel.
  • For each pixel the shader reads alpha at 16 points in a disc of 7 px. The share of points inside the shape is the height: 1 well inside, about 0.5 on the edge. The average of the points' offsets, weighted by alpha, points away from the nearest edge. That gives a normal without a second pass.
  • Labels are embossed with a second, smaller slope taken from the brightness of the picture.
  • The shadow is the same alpha read 16 px towards the light, through 8 jittered samples.
  • The seven keys of the keypad are one picture. A pressed key is scaled to 0.9 by :active, which changes the alpha, and the lighting follows with no code for it.

Findings

From Chromium 157 with software rendering. The rows above say what your browser does.

  • Works: every outline is in the alpha channel. corner-shape (squircle, bevel, scoop, notch, superellipse), border-shape: circle() and clip-path: shape() all change the picture the shader receives, so one shader lights all of them.
  • Works: normals from 16 samples. The bevel is smooth at 7 px. Below about 3 px the samples land less than a pixel apart and the bevel becomes a plain edge highlight. Above about 14 px the 16 samples show as faint steps.
  • Hit testing follows all three outlines. A point in a corner that corner-shape, border-shape or clip-path cut away is outside the element for elementFromPoint(), in a canvas and as plain DOM. A click in the gap between a piece's box and its outline doesn't press it. The shader moves no pixels, so no geometry update is needed.
  • Limit: the shader can't see behind a piece. A shadow is drawn in the canvas of the piece that casts it, inside 30 px of extra canvas round the piece. It doesn't darken a neighbour that is itself a canvas above it.
  • Not verified here: the tilt sensor (the test browser has none), and the frame rate on a phone, where each piece costs 29 texture reads per pixel while the light moves.
